misconceptions.label: All cells look the same
misconceptions.nova_says: I think all cells are the same shape and size, like identical bricks. So a nerve cell and a muscle cell look exactly alike, right?
misconceptions.correct_idea: Cells vary in shape and size, and each cell's shape suits its function: a nerve cell is long and branched to carry messages, muscle cells are spindle shaped to contract.
misconceptions.probe: Why would a nerve cell need a different shape from a muscle cell?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Can you give me an example of two cells with different shapes?

misconceptions.label: Cell wall and cell membrane are the same
misconceptions.nova_says: Cell wall and cell membrane are just two names for the same thing. Every cell, even mine, has a hard cell wall!
misconceptions.correct_idea: The cell membrane is a thin porous layer around every cell that controls what enters and leaves. Only plant cells (and some bacteria and fungi) also have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane, for extra protection and support.
wrong_signals: animal cells have a cell wall
misconceptions.probe: Which cells have a cell wall, and which only have a membrane?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What does the cell membrane do that the wall does not?

misconceptions.label: The nucleus is the whole cell's only important part
misconceptions.nova_says: Only the nucleus matters. The cytoplasm is just water filling the space, it doesn't do anything.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The nucleus controls the cell's activities and carries chromosomes with genes, but the cytoplasm is where many of the cell's activities happen and holds organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes and plastids.
misconceptions.probe: If the cytoplasm did nothing, where would the cell's other parts sit and work?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Can you name something that is found in the cytoplasm?

misconceptions.label: Moving objects need a force to keep moving
misconceptions.nova_says: A rolling ball stops because the force inside it runs out. Things only move while a force keeps pushing them.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A force changes the state of motion. A rolling ball slows down and stops because friction acts against its motion; without friction it would keep moving.
wrong_signals: needs a push to keep moving
misconceptions.probe: What force acts on the ball while it rolls on the ground?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Would the ball roll further on smooth ice? Why?

misconceptions.label: Pressure is the same as force
misconceptions.nova_says: Pressure and force are the same thing. A sharp knife and a blunt knife press just as hard if I push the same.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Pressure is force per unit area. The same force on a smaller area, like a sharp edge, gives a bigger pressure, so a sharp knife cuts more easily.
misconceptions.probe: What is different about the edge of a sharp knife compared with a blunt one?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Why do porters put a round cloth on their heads?

misconceptions.label: Forces need contact
misconceptions.nova_says: A force can only work if two things touch. A magnet can't pull a pin that it isn't touching.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Non-contact forces act without touching: magnetic force, electrostatic force and the force of gravity act from a distance.
misconceptions.probe: What happens when you bring a magnet close to pins without touching them?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Can you name another force that works from a distance?

misconceptions.label: Friction is always bad
misconceptions.nova_says: Friction is always bad. We should remove all friction everywhere.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Friction is a necessary evil: it wears things out and wastes energy as heat, but without friction we could not walk, write or hold things, and vehicles could not stop.
misconceptions.probe: What would happen if you tried to walk on a floor with no friction?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Give me one place where friction helps us.

misconceptions.label: Sound travels through empty space
misconceptions.nova_says: Astronauts can shout to each other in space, because sound travels everywhere, even where there is no air.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through a vacuum, so in space astronauts use radios.
misconceptions.probe: What does sound need to travel through?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What happens to the sound of a bell when air is pumped out of the jar?

misconceptions.label: Loud sounds are high-pitched
misconceptions.nova_says: Loudness and pitch are the same. A loud drum has a very high pitch.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration; pitch depends on frequency. A sound can be loud and low-pitched, like a lion's roar.
misconceptions.probe: What property of a vibration decides loudness, and what decides pitch?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Can you think of a sound that is loud but low-pitched?

misconceptions.label: Eyes send out light to see
misconceptions.nova_says: We see things because our eyes send out rays that hit objects.
misconceptions.correct_idea: We see an object when light coming from it, usually light reflected from it, enters our eyes.
misconceptions.probe: Can you see objects in a completely dark room? Why not?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Where does the light that reaches your eyes come from?

misconceptions.label: Angles measured from the mirror
misconceptions.nova_says: The angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface, not from anything else.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the normal, the line drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror at the point of incidence, and they are equal.
misconceptions.probe: What is the normal, and why do we use it?
misconceptions.example_prompt: If the angle of incidence is 30 degrees, what is the angle of reflection?

misconceptions.label: Anything burns once lit
misconceptions.nova_says: If I hold a match to anything, it will start burning straight away.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A substance burns only when it is combustible, there is air (oxygen), and it is heated to its ignition temperature.
misconceptions.probe: Why does a paper cup of water not burn when heated?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What three things are needed for burning?

misconceptions.label: Water puts out every fire
misconceptions.nova_says: Water can put out any fire, even an oil fire or an electrical fire.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Water is not suitable for oil or electrical fires: oil floats on water and keeps burning, and water conducts electricity. Carbon dioxide is used instead, because it cuts off the supply of air.
misconceptions.probe: What happens to oil when you pour water on it?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What is used to put out an electrical fire?

misconceptions.label: All microbes are harmful
misconceptions.nova_says: All microorganisms are germs that make us sick, so we should kill every single one.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Many microorganisms are useful: yeast makes bread rise, Lactobacillus turns milk into curd, some make antibiotics, and bacteria fix nitrogen in soil. Only some cause disease.
misconceptions.probe: Can you name a food that is made with the help of microorganisms?
misconceptions.example_prompt: How does curd form from milk?

misconceptions.label: Antibiotics cure viral infections
misconceptions.nova_says: When I have a cold or flu, I should take antibiotics to kill the virus.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses. They do not cure colds or flu, and should be taken only when a doctor prescribes them.
misconceptions.probe: What kind of microorganism do antibiotics work against?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Who should decide when you take antibiotics?

misconceptions.label: All metals are hard and solid
misconceptions.nova_says: All metals are hard solids and all non-metals are soft.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Most metals are hard, but sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife, and mercury is a liquid at room temperature. Diamond, a non-metal form of carbon, is very hard.
misconceptions.probe: Can you think of a metal that is not a hard solid?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?

misconceptions.label: Shelter under a tall tree in lightning
misconceptions.nova_says: During lightning, the safest place is under a tall tree.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Tall trees attract lightning, so sheltering under one is unsafe. A closed building or car is safer; in the open, crouch low away from tall objects.
wrong_signals: safest place is under a tree
under a tall tree is safe
misconceptions.probe: Why might lightning strike a tall tree first?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Where would you go to stay safe in a thunderstorm?

misconceptions.label: Phases are caused by Earth's shadow
misconceptions.nova_says: The moon has phases because the Earth's shadow covers part of it every night.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The moon does not make its own light. Phases occur because we see only the part of the moon's sunlit half that faces us, which changes as the moon goes around the Earth.
misconceptions.probe: Does the moon make its own light?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Why do we see a full moon only on some nights?

misconceptions.label: Clear water is always safe
misconceptions.nova_says: If water looks clear and clean, it is safe to drink.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Clear water can still carry germs and dissolved harmful substances. Water must be purified, for example by filtering, boiling or chlorination, to make it potable.
misconceptions.probe: Can water look clear but still carry germs?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What can you do at home to make water safe to drink?

misconceptions.label: Fossil fuels will never run out
misconceptions.nova_says: Coal and petroleum will never run out, because the Earth keeps making more.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Coal and petroleum are exhaustible resources. They formed from dead organisms over millions of years, so they cannot be replaced in our lifetime and must be used carefully.
misconceptions.probe: How long did it take for coal to form?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What is one way to save petrol?

misconceptions.label: All plastics break down quickly
misconceptions.nova_says: Plastic bags rot away in the soil in a few weeks, like banana peels.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Most plastics are non-biodegradable: bacteria cannot break them down, so they stay in the environment for many years. We should reduce, reuse, recycle and recover.
misconceptions.probe: Can bacteria break down plastic the way they break down peels?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What can we do with plastic instead of throwing it away?

misconceptions.label: More fertiliser is always better
misconceptions.nova_says: If a little fertiliser helps, then adding loads more will always grow bigger crops.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Too much fertiliser harms the soil and pollutes water. Manure adds humus and improves soil texture, and crop rotation with pulses restores nitrogen naturally.
misconceptions.probe: What happens to the soil if too much fertiliser is used?
misconceptions.example_prompt: How can farmers add nitrogen without fertilisers?

misconceptions.label: Cutting trees only affects wood supply
misconceptions.nova_says: Cutting forests only means we have less wood. It doesn't change anything else.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Deforestation reduces rainfall, increases soil erosion, floods and droughts, raises carbon dioxide in the air and can turn land into desert.
misconceptions.probe: What holds the soil in place in a forest?
misconceptions.example_prompt: How could cutting trees change the rain in an area?

misconceptions.label: Every animal needs two parents
misconceptions.nova_says: Every animal needs two parents to make a young one.
misconceptions.correct_idea: In asexual reproduction only one parent is involved: Hydra reproduces by budding and Amoeba by binary fission.
misconceptions.probe: How does a Hydra make a new Hydra?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What happens when an Amoeba divides?

misconceptions.label: The mother decides the baby's sex
misconceptions.nova_says: The mother decides whether the baby will be a boy or a girl.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The sex of the baby depends on the sex chromosome in the father's sperm that fertilises the egg: an X gives a girl (XX) and a Y gives a boy (XY). The egg always carries an X.
misconceptions.probe: Which sex chromosome does every egg carry?
misconceptions.example_prompt: What combination of chromosomes gives a girl?

misconceptions.label: All water conducts electricity
misconceptions.nova_says: All water conducts electricity well, even pure distilled water.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Distilled water is a poor conductor. Tap water conducts because it contains dissolved salts; solutions of acids, bases and salts conduct electricity.
misconceptions.probe: What happens when you add salt to distilled water and test it?
misconceptions.example_prompt: Why is it dangerous to touch switches with wet hands?

ai_moments.claim: NOVA's photo-recognition app labels a plant cell with no cell wall as 'animal cell'. It is 99% confident.
ai_moments.question: What should you do with NOVA's 99% confident label?
options: Check it against what you know: a plant cell has a cell wall and large vacuole
Ask NOVA again until it changes its answer
ai_moments.explanation: High confidence is not proof. Check AI claims against evidence you know is true.

ai_moments.claim: An AI noticed that more ice creams are sold on days with more drownings and concluded ice cream causes drowning.
ai_moments.question: What is wrong with the AI's conclusion?
options: Both rise on hot days; a pattern is not proof of cause
The AI needs more ice cream data
ai_moments.explanation: A pattern in data (correlation) does not mean one thing causes the other.

ai_moments.claim: A voice assistant mishears quiet speakers more often than loud ones.
ai_moments.question: Which property of sound is the assistant struggling with?
ai_moments.explanation: Quiet speech has small amplitude, so the microphone gets weaker data to recognise.

ai_moments.claim: A self-driving car camera works badly in fog and darkness.
ai_moments.question: Why does the camera struggle?
options: Cameras need light from objects to reach them, just like eyes
Cameras send out rays that fog blocks
ai_moments.explanation: Like our eyes, a camera can only record light that reaches it from objects.

8.1.explain: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under a simple microscope. He saw tiny box-like compartments separated by walls, like a honeycomb, and called each box a 'cell'. The cork cells were actually dead. Better microscopes later let scientists study living cells.
8.1.explain_again: Think of a honeycomb: many small rooms with walls between them. That is what Hooke saw in cork. He named each little room a cell, a word that means a small room.
8.1.example: Worked example: Why did it take 150 years to learn more about cells after Hooke? Step 1: cells are far too small to see with the naked eye. Step 2: early microscopes had low magnification. Step 3: so progress waited for better microscopes.

checks.q: What did Robert Hooke observe under his microscope?
checks.why: Hooke looked at thin slices of cork, which is part of the bark of a tree.

checks.q: The cells Hooke saw in cork were…
checks.why: Cork cells are dead; only their walls remain, which is why they looked like empty boxes.

8.2.explain: Just as bricks are the units that build a house, cells are the basic structural units of every living organism. Organisms differ from one another, but all are made of cells. Unlike bricks, cells are complex and alive.
8.2.explain_again: If you zoom into any living thing, a leaf, your skin, a fish, you will always reach cells, the smallest living building blocks.
8.2.example: Worked example: Is a hen's egg a cell? The egg (without its shell) is a single cell, one of the largest cells we can see without a microscope.

checks.q: Why are cells compared to bricks?
options: Both are basic units that build something larger
checks.why: Cells build organisms the way bricks build buildings, though cells are alive.

checks.q: Which of these is a single cell you can see without a microscope?
checks.why: A hen's egg is a single large cell.

8.3.explain: Some organisms, like Amoeba and Paramecium, are made of a single cell (unicellular). Others, like us, are made of billions of cells (multicellular). Cells also vary in shape and size. Amoeba changes shape using pseudopodia; a nerve cell is long and branched to carry messages; white blood cells can change shape.
8.3.explain_again: Cells are like workers with different uniforms for different jobs. A nerve cell is long like a wire to carry messages; a muscle cell is spindle shaped so it can contract.
8.3.example: Worked example: Does an elephant have bigger cells than a rat? No. Cell size is not related to the size of the animal; the elephant simply has many more cells.

checks.q: An organism made of a single cell is called…
checks.why: Uni means one: Amoeba and Paramecium are unicellular.

checks.q: Why is a nerve cell long and branched?
checks.why: Its long branched shape suits its job of receiving and transferring messages.

checks.q: An elephant's cells compared with a rat's cells are…
options: Not related to the animal's size
checks.why: Cell size does not depend on body size; the elephant has more cells, not bigger ones.

8.4.explain: In multicellular organisms, groups of similar cells working together form a tissue, and tissues make up organs. Each cell's structure suits its function: muscle cells contract and relax, nerve cells carry messages.
8.4.explain_again: Cells are like players in a team. Similar players form a group (tissue), and groups together run the whole show (organ).
8.4.example: Worked example: Put in order from smallest to largest: organ, cell, tissue. Answer: cell → tissue → organ.

checks.q: A group of similar cells performing a function is called…
checks.why: Similar cells working together form a tissue.

8.5.explain: A cell has three main parts. The cell membrane is a thin porous layer that encloses the cell and controls what goes in and out. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance between membrane and nucleus where organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes and plastids sit. The nucleus, usually near the centre, controls the cell's activities and holds chromosomes that carry genes. Plant cells also have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane, plastids such as chloroplasts, and a large vacuole.
8.5.explain_again: Think of a school. The boundary wall with a gate is the membrane, deciding who enters. The playground and classrooms are the cytoplasm, where activities happen. The principal's office is the nucleus, giving instructions.
8.5.example: Worked example: Onion peel stained with iodine. Step 1: the boundary of each cell is visible. Step 2: a dark dot in each cell is the nucleus, stained by iodine. Step 3: the outer thick layer is the cell wall, so it is a plant cell.

checks.q: Which part controls the activities of the cell?
checks.why: The nucleus is the control centre and carries chromosomes.

checks.q: Which part allows some substances in and out of the cell?
checks.why: The porous cell membrane controls movement of materials.
Chromosomes in the nucleus carry genes, which pass characters from parents to offspring.

8.6.explain: Plant and animal cells both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. Only plant cells have a cell wall and plastids (including green chloroplasts), and plant cells usually have one large vacuole, while animal cells have small vacuoles or none.
8.6.explain_again: A plant cell is like an animal cell wearing an extra hard jacket (cell wall), carrying solar panels (chloroplasts) and a big water tank (large vacuole).
8.6.example: Worked example: A cell has a cell wall and chloroplasts. Is it from a leaf or from cheek lining? It has a cell wall and chloroplasts, which only plant cells have, so it is from a leaf.

checks.q: Which part is found only in plant cells?
checks.why: Animal cells have no cell wall.

checks.q: Which structure gives leaves their green colour?
checks.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green pigment.
